content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on convergence analysis of adversarial training for finite-width two-layer Leaky ReLU networks. Convergence guarantees are given for both inner-loop PGD-style adversarial attack (in deterministic form) and end-to-end adversarial training with imperfect attack (in expectation form). To ease the analysis, the framework focuses on binary classification setting with only first-layer weights updatable. Moreover, in the inner-loop attack, authors propose a lower bound of 0-1 loss as the surrogate and the training gradients use the classical binary sigmoid loss as the surrogate. Lastly, the lower bound surrogate loss is demonstrated to be effective in practice (on MNIST, CIFAR-10).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Strong theoretical guarantees of adversarial training under loose assumptions. Theorem 4 establishes the convergence of adversarial training in terms of a small expected error of large-margin adversarial examples, for finite-width two-layer Leaky-ReLU networks. These results seem to be the first of this kind. Technically, the proof relies on the monotonicity of gradients - a specific mathematical property of the well-designed surrogate loss along with telescoping cancellation, which is not straightforward.

- The paper also establishes the deterministic convergence guarantee for adversarial training.

- The proposed lower bound surrogate loss for the adversarial attack is effective in practice which may of independent interests.

- The writing quality in the main text is great and it is easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
- The analysis is limited in the following aspects: (1) The analyzed two-layer neural network does not allow the weight evolvement in the second-layer, which is different from the adversarial training practice. (2) The latent assumption of linear separation (second point of Asumption 3.3) seems strong. (3) Extension of the analysis to multi-class settings may be hard.

- The proof can be made more rigorous. For instance, I got lost in the following places:

  1. Proof of Thm 3.2: Let $G := ||W||_F$ and $\kappa \sqrt m ||W||_F =: G$ seem to be contradicting.
  2. Proof of Thm 3.2, page 13 upper part: how does average case guarantee $\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T -\ell_- (yf_W(\delta_t)) \le ...$ lead to single instance guarantee $-\ell_-(yf_W(\delta_{att})) \le ...$? From the bottom of page 13, it seems to be because $-\ell_-(yf_W(\delta_{att})) = \min_{t\in[T]} -\ell_-(yf_W(\delta_t))$. However, why is this guaranteed? Since it is a project GD, when the step size is sufficiently small I can see it holds, but does it hold generally?
  3. Proof of Lemma 3.7, page 14: why is it an equality in $y_t \sum_{r=1}^m \langle a_r \sigma'(w_r \cdot \delta)\delta, \frac{1}{\sqrt m} \mathrm{sgn}(a_r)v_* \rangle = \frac{\kappa}{\sqrt m} \sum_{r=1}^m \sigma'(w_r\cdot \delta) y_t\langle \delta, v_*\rangle$? We only know $||a||_{\infty} \le \kappa$ but does it lead to $a_r = \kappa$ for any $r$?
  4. Proof of Lemma 3.7, bottom of page 15: how does $\tau \le ...$ connect to $T \le ...$? If I understand correctly, we need $T \ge \lceil \tau \rceil + 1$ to lead to contradiction. But here, RHS of $\tau \le ...$ seems to be squared which may not imply $T \ge \lceil \tau \rceil + 1$.

- How does this convergence-guaranteed adversarial training of two-layer DNN compare to exact-convex-opt-solving-based adversarial training (e.g., [1])?

[1] Bai, Yatong, Tanmay Gautam, and Somayeh Sojoudi. "Efficient global optimization of two-layer relu networks: Quadratic-time algorithms and adversarial training." arXiv preprint arXiv:2201.01965 (2022).


Minor:
1. After Definition 3.1, "in terms of the and the negated loss derivative": missing noun
2. After Theorem 3.2, $O(\beta^2 / \epsilon)$ iteration may need further justification
3. Section 4.1 may be moved to appendix to gain space for proof sketching of Thm. 3.2 and Lemma 3.7
4. Table 2's result is hard to parse. Why larger attack steps for RA columns can lead to significantly larger robust accuracy? Also, what does SA mean? When attach size $\nu$ is specified in the table, how is it different from caption of Table 2 which says $\nu = 8/255$?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarify and quality of the main text is generally great. The result is novel to the best of my knowledge. However, some steps in the appendix proof may be unclear.
content.summary_of_the_review: Though I got lost in some steps of the proofs, assuming that the proofs are all correct and will be revised clear, and the related work is discussed comprehensively (I'm not working in DL theory so cannot evaluate this aspect), I think the contribution is sufficient, of interest to the community, and worth acceptance - the results further our theoretical understanding of adversarial training.

content.title: detailed feedback on the reviewer comments
content.comment:
Thank you for reading our proofs!

 - Thanks for catching the typo, a factor of $\kappa \sqrt{m}$ is missing. We emphasize that $G:= \kappa \sqrt{m} ||W||_F$ as defined in the last line of the first set of equations in Proof of Theorem 3.2., and used in third-from-last inequality at the bottom of page 12. 

- $\delta_{atk}$ is by definition (Algorithm 1, “Output” line) is the argmin of iterates. Because the minimum is always smaller than the average, this inequality always holds true.

- Thanks for the catch! We acknowledge that we’ve misstated the initialization of the top layer weights; it should be initialized as Uniform({+\kappa, -\kappa}). Such uniform initialization is standard in the analysis of gradient-based methods in deep learning, see e.g. https://openreview.net/pdf?id=HygegyrYwH or https://arxiv.org/pdf/1810.02054.pdf or https://arxiv.org/pdf/2101.01152.pdf or  https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.10174.pdf. We emphasize that does not change any of our main results.

- The goal is to show that “for any $\epsilon$, there exists an iterate $t$ such that $-\mathbb{E} \ell'(y_t f_{\delta_t}(W_t))\leq \epsilon$". Assuming otherwise, i.e. assuming all iterates have expected $\ell’(\cdot)$ bigger than $\epsilon$, then we arrive at an upperbound on $\tau$, that is, the expected $\ell’(\cdot)$ cannot continue to be bigger than $\epsilon$ for more than $\tau$ iterates. This gives an upperbound on $T$, the total number of iterations need to run the algorithm.

- Comparison with https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.01965.pdf: thanks for bringing this work to our attention! While there's no direct comparison between the convex-programing approach in [1] and the direct, non-convex analysis we adopt in this submission, we will add a discussion around this line of study in general and the specific work suggested by you.

content.title: on linear separability and significance of the experimental results
content.comment:
Thanks for the review. Please see below our feedback.

- "What is the point of robustness of neural networks models for linearly separable data… what are the new contributions": 
      Our problem setting is arguably way more challenging due to leaky ReLU non-linearities. We address two open theoretical questions, 1) can PGD find a label-flipping attack, when there exists one; and 2) can adversarial training find a robust solution? Both questions are non-trivial and the answers were unknown before this work. Linear separability is a strong assumption; however, we note that PGD attack in Theorem 3.2 does not require linear realizability – this is the first of its kind result and one of the main contributions. We do require linear realizability but only for convergence of adversarial training. Here also, even in the non-robust setting, we require linear realizability for computational tractability; note that in general training neural networks are hard (refer to the paragraph following Assumption 3.3).

 - "The results of the experiment are not significantly good":
       That’s why nowhere in the paper do we claim that reflecting the loss will improve adversarial training for general deep neural networks. This is a theoretical investigation into the dynamics of adversarial training, where we also provide strong supporting empirical evidence that reflecting the loss doesn’t hurt the performance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the robust adversarial learning problem for a binary classification task, where the standard adversary's logistic loss function is reflected around the origin. Specifically, the classifier is chosen to be a one-hidden layer neural network with leaky-ReLU activation, and the two classes are assumed to be linearly separable. Under these assumptions, the paper proves a convergence guarantee for the projected gradient descent optimization algorithm. The paper presents some numerical results on binary and multi-class classification problems to support the proposed bi-level adversarial training approach and the shown convergence results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1) The paper is well-written and the presentation is satisfactory.

2) The idea of reflecting the surrogate logistic loss around the origin sounds highly interesting to me, since it resolves the non-concavity of the surrogate loss in the adversary's maximization problem. The idea seems to be potentially useful for other theoretical analyses of adversarial training problems as well. 

Weaknesses:

1) The paper's convergence analysis is based on two relatively strong assumptions: 1) the analysis targets a binary classification problem and its extension to multi-class classification problems looks challenging, 2) the two classes are supposed to be linearly separable.

2) While I very much like the reflection idea for the inner maximization problem, this change leads to a different bi-level optimization problem from the standard min-max adversarial training problem. Therefore, while the paper's introduction sets the goal of understanding the convergence properties of robust adversarial training, the proposed framework deviates from standard robust training approaches. 
I am wondering what the results of the paper could imply about the convergence of standard min-max adversarial training.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written, and the analysis and results look novel to me.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a new approach to robust adversarial training by proposing a novel bi-level optimization problem based on reflecting the maximization surrogate loss function around the origin. While the analysis is restricted to binary classification problems with linearly separable classes, I think the paper contributes interesting ideas for analyzing adversarial training problems.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: extension to the multi class setting, linear separability, and difference in objectives
content.comment:
Thanks for the review. Please see below our feedback.

- "two relatively strong assumptions ...  extension to multi-class classification problems looks challenging": 
       Extension to multi-class setting is an interesting open question that we leave for future work, as we discuss in the second paragraph of the Discussion section. We do however provide an empirical study in Section 4.3., where we touch on the challenges involved as well as provide a greedy approach that shows competitive performance in terms of standard/adversarial test error

 - "the two classes are supposed to be linearly separable": 
       Linear separability is a strong assumption; however, we note that PGD attack in Theorem 3.2 does not require linear realizability – this is the first of its kind result and one of the main contributions. We do require linear realizability but only for convergence of adversarial training. Here also, even in the non-robust setting, we require linear realizability for computational tractability; note that in general training neural networks are hard (refer to the paragraph following Assumption 3.3). 

 - "this change leads to a different bi-level optimization problem from the standard min-max adversarial training problem": 
       it is indeed a different bi-level optimization however 1) it comes at absolutely no additional computational cost; 2) it is intuitive as theoretically motivated; 3) it does not hurt the performance. Finally, please note that minimizing the robust misclassification error (i.e. Equation (1) *is* the holy-grail of robust training; standard adversarial training is just one (very interesting) heuristic to approach this problem. We do firmly believe that investigating other theoretically-motivated formulations can potentially improve state of the art.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper analyzes theoretically the robustness of adversarial training of two layer neural network.
The analysis is done on a linearly separable dataset through slightly modifying the objective of PGD attacks.
Experimental analysis of the proposed modification of PGD attacks are carried our on small scale problems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strength of this paper is the theoretical analysis presented in section 3. It is very useful to analyze the convergence of such popular approach in building robust models to allow theoretically supported robustness enhancements. However, there are key concerns about the effectiveness of this work:

- First, the experimental results are very limited to very small scale problems. The argument of this work would have been much stronger if it was demonstrated on standard robustness benchmarks showing robustness improvements.

- The analysis presented in sections 2 and 3 assumes Leaky ReLU activation function, while the experiments are carried out on ReLU-based networks. However, substituting $\alpha \rightarrow 0$ in Theorem 3.4 would yield $T_{tr} \leq \infty$. That is, if I understood correctly, Theorem 3.4 does not bring useful conclusions about adversarial training  under the experimental setup even when using a two-layer network. Please correct me if I am missing something in the previous argument.

- The assumptions in the theoretical analysis limit the usefulness of the results. For instance, why is the weights of the second linear layer, $i.e.$ are kept fixed? In Assumption 3.3, the input space is assumed to be bounded. However, $R$ could be extremely large in reality $e.g. R=(255)\sqrt{d}$ for images where $d$ is the number of pixels. This would result in an extremely small learning rate as per Theorem 3.4.

Minor concerns:

- The writing of the paper can be further improved. There are few typos such as: "in terms of the and..." in page 4. 

- Table 1 is hard to read. Please consider highlighting main number in the table with stating the main message in the caption.

- The proof sketch in section 3.1 seems a bit disconnected from the rest of the paper. Please consider moving it to the appendix.

- The main result of this work (Theorem 3.4) is about the convergence guarantees of adversarial training. Please consider reflecting that into the title as robustness guarantees usually refers to some sort of certified robustness.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The claims in this work as clear and novel in some aspects. However, the presented results have limited impact.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My main concerns about this work are: (1) The limited experimental analysis. (2) The mismatch between the theoretical results and the experimental setup. (3) The usefulness of the theoretical results under the stated assumptions. 
Please refer to the review for more details.

content.title: 1) empirical study aims to generalize the scope of the theory, 2) assumptions are standard.
content.comment:
Thanks for the review. Please see below our feedback.
 - "the experimental results are very limited to very small scale problems":
       We present a theoretical study of adversarial training and the goal of the experimental section is to support and generalize the scope of the theory. Nowhere in this article do we claim that the reflected loss substantially improves performance.

 - "analysis assumes Leaky ReLU activation, while the experiments are carried out on ReLU-based networks":
       The goal is to empirically evaluate the reflected loss for ReLU activation function which is way more popular than leaky ReLU. There’s nothing wrong in showing that an idea can be generalized beyond the theoretical setting.

 - "assumptions in the theoretical analysis limit the usefulness of the results ... why is the weights of the second linear layer, are kept fixed?"
       This is standard in theoretical deep learning (see e.g. https://openreview.net/pdf?id=HygegyrYwH or https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.06668.pdf and the references therein).

 - "the input space is assumed to be bounded": 
       This is standard in theoretical machine learning and optimization theory, see e.g. Learning Theory textbooks https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/~shais/UnderstandingMachineLearning/understanding-machine-learning-theory-algorithms.pdf or SGD analysis papers such as https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.10174.pdf. In fact, many papers simply assume $\|x\| = 1$ for all datapoints, which is even stronger, see e.g. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.06668.pdf, or https://arxiv.org/pdf/1810.02054.pdf, or https://openreview.net/pdf?id=HygegyrYwH or https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.08888.pdf or https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.03804.pdf. BTW, for the case of a d-dimensional image, the upperbound on the norm would be $255 \sqrt{d}$, not $255^d$.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper studies adversarial training on shallow Leaky ReLU networks under a linear separability assumption, and is able to prove guarantees using a modified adversarial attack.  Reviewers were almost exactly borderline, and discussion also was heavily borderline. 
 Unfortunately, due to the high bar at ICLR this year, a final calibration put this paper just microscopically away from the decision boundary, on the reject side.  We apologize for this disappointment, and urge the authors to refine their work and submit to a future venue.

One concern that arose late in the review phase was that the proof is very closely related to prior work due to Frei et al., to the extent that here is some concern that the modified loss was reverse engineered to allow that proof to go through.  Furthermore, it's not clear why this proof technique requires linear separability (plus noise).  We hope that these comments, plus various reviewer comments, can all be addressed by the authors to make their work even more exciting and a clear accept at a future venue.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The assumptions are very strong (linear separability with smaller adversarial perturbations), and the proof and technical content are highly reliant on a proof in similar settings by Frei et al (as cited in this work).  Indeed the paper seems highly incremental from that prior work, and while it constitutes definite progress, I feel this incremental nature contributed to the (consistent!) indecision of the reviewers.
